mainTopic: בגדי כהונה: wrong-length garments, the יתר question through ציצית, and what ״בַּד״ teaches
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא: serving in dirty or torn בגדי כהונה makes the עבודה פסולה. שמואל rules that clothes that drag (מרושלין) are כשר, but clothes that are raised (מסולקין) are פסול. רמי בר חמא resolves a contradicting ברייתא: hitched up with the אבנט is כשר, while too short from the start is פסול. רב holds that both too long and too short are פסול, and רבי זירא explains that רב read the ברייתא as one case: long garments pulled up with the אבנט. רבי ירמיה מדיפתי tries to tie unraised long garments to a תנאים dispute about a five-cornered garment and ציצית, asking whether something extra counts. The גמרא rejects this: both תנאים hold that the extra counts, and they really argue about how to read ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״. Next, a ברייתא lists what the word ״בַּד״ teaches, and רב יוסף explains that some of these features are only ideal while others are required. The גמרא then proves that ״בַּד״ means flax, and the amud ends with אביי's explanation of ״לֹא יַחְגְּרוּ בַּיָּזַע״ and a ברייתא about where the belt is tied, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Dirty or torn priestly clothes disqualify the service
steps.stepSummary: This line finishes a ברייתא: if a כהן serves in dirty or torn בגדי כהונה, his עבודה is פסולה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the clothes were dirty or torn and he did the service, his service is disqualified.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא that started just before this point. It says that serving in dirty or torn priestly clothes ruins the עבודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that a כהן must serve in proper בגדי כהונה. Clothes that are dirty or ripped do not count as proper, so the עבודה done in them is פסולה. The next steps move on to a related question: what about clothes that are the wrong length?

keyTerms.meaning: The sacrificial service done by a כהן

phrases.english: If they were soiled or ripped
and he performed the service, his service is disqualified.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְטוּשְׁטָשִׁין אוֹ מְקוֹרָעִין וְעָבַד עֲבוֹדָתוֹ פְּסוּלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a ברייתא that started before this point.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Service done in dirty or torn בגדי כהונה is פסולה.

steps.title: שמואל: dragging clothes are fine, raised clothes are not
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes שמואל: if the בגדי כהונה drag on the ground (מרושלין) they are כשר, but if they are raised up too high (מסולקין) they are פסול.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: If the clothes drag on the ground, they are valid. If they are raised up, they are invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a new rule about the length of the priestly clothes. Too long is fine, but too short is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Clothes that are too long still fully cover the כהן, so שמואל counts them as כשר. Clothes that sit too high do not reach where they should, so he counts them as פסול. This ruling is about to be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: Raised up, sitting too high (too short)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says that Shmuel says:
If they are dragging on the ground, they are fit,
if they are raised up, they are unfit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from dirty or torn clothes to clothes that are the wrong length.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Clothes that are too long are כשר; clothes that are raised up too high are פסול.

steps.title: A ברייתא says raised clothes are fit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: a ברייתא teaches that מסולקין are כשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches: if they are raised up, they are valid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל's ruling by quoting a ברייתא that says the opposite about raised-up clothes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said מסולקין are פסול, but the ברייתא says מסולקין are כשר. A ברייתא carries great authority, so this looks like a direct contradiction.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: If they are raised up, they are fit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's ruling in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that מסולקין are פסול.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא rules that מסולקין are כשר, which directly contradicts שמואל.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא: hitched up versus too short from the start
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא resolves the contradiction. The ברייתא means clothes of the right length that were pulled up with the אבנט. שמואל means clothes that never reached the right length at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: It is not difficult. Here (the ברייתא) is when he raised them up with his belt. There (שמואל) is when they were never long enough to begin with.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא shows that the ברייתא and שמואל are talking about two different cases, so they do not really argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the clothes are really the right length and the כהן just hitched them up with his אבנט, they are still proper clothes, so they are כשר. If the clothes were made too short from the start, they are not proper clothes, so they are פסול. The word מסולקין can describe both cases, and each source is talking about a different one.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (introduces an answer)

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the two "כאן" (here) lines. The first one, hitched up by the אבנט, matches the ברייתא (כשר). The second one, too short from the start, matches שמואל (פסול).
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer comes back at the end of the piece. רב הונא relies on it instead of giving his own answer.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: לָא קַשְׁיָא;
phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama says: This is not difficult;
here, it is where he raised them up by means of the belt,
there, it is where they do not reach at all from the start.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source is talking about a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the ברייתא and שמואל were talking about the same kind of raised-up clothes and disagreed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means properly sized clothes hitched up by the אבנט (כשר). שמואל means clothes that were too short from the start (פסול).

steps.title: רב: both too long and too short are unfit
steps.stepSummary: רב disagrees with שמואל and holds that both מרושלין and מסולקין are פסול.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Both this and that, dragging and raised up, are invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives his own opinion, which is stricter than שמואל's. To him, clothes of the wrong length in either direction disqualify the עבודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל allowed clothes that are too long. רב does not. In his view the clothes must be the exact right length, and too long or too short are both פסול.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this one and that one

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה – פְּסוּלִין.
phrases.english: Rav says: Both this and that are unfit.
phrases.notes: "This and that" means the dragging clothes and the raised-up clothes from שמואל's ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה פְּסוּלִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different opinion from שמואל's in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Clothes that are too long or too short are both פסול.

steps.title: The innkeeper's son challenges רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא came to ארגיזא, and his innkeeper's son raised the same contradiction between שמואל and the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא came to ארגיזא. The son of his innkeeper asked him: Did שמואל really say that dragging clothes are valid and raised clothes are invalid? But a ברייתא teaches that raised clothes are valid!
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short story. A local person brings רב הונא the same challenge the גמרא raised in step 3.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is the same as before: שמואל says מסולקין are פסול, but the ברייתא says they are כשר. The story shows how well known this contradiction was.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised a contradiction to him

phrases.english: Rav Huna happened to come to Argiza,
the son of his innkeeper raised a contradiction to him:
Did Shmuel really say that dragging clothes are fit
and raised-up clothes are unfit?!
But isn't it taught: If they are raised up, they are fit!

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא אִיקְּלַע לְאַרְגִּיזָא רְמָא לֵיהּ בַּר אוּשְׁפִּיזְכָנֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to שמואל's ruling and repeats the challenge of step 3 inside a story.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that מסולקין are פסול.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says מסולקין are כשר, which contradicts שמואל.

steps.title: רב הונא: that one was already answered
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers that this ברייתא is no problem, because רמי בר חמא already explained it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Bring me anything except that ברייתא, because רמי בר חמא already explained it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא does not give a new answer. He points back to רמי בר חמא's answer from step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רמי בר חמא already showed that the ברייתא is about clothes hitched up by the אבנט, while שמואל is about clothes that were too short from the start. So the ברייתא does not contradict שמואל, and רב הונא tells the young man to look for a different challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: He answered it, he explained it differently

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל: clothes that are too long are כשר; clothes that are too short from the start are פסול; clothes of the right length that were hitched up with the אבנט are כשר (רמי בר חמא). רב: too long and too short are both פסול.

phrases.english: He said to him: Apart from that one,
since Rami bar Ḥama already answered it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּר מִינַּהּ דְּהַהִיא דְּשַׁנְּיַיהּ רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the innkeeper's son's challenge in step 6 by pointing to step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points back to an answer that was already given (רמי בר חמא's split between the two cases).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The innkeeper's son thought the ברייתא disproves שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא was already explained by רמי בר חמא, so שמואל's ruling stands.

steps.title: The ברייתא is a problem for רב
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says מרושלין and מסולקין are כשר, but רב says both are פסול. Reading מרושלין as long garments pulled up by the אבנט fixes only half, because מסולקין is still a problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for רב the ברייתא is difficult! And if you say that 'dragging' means garments raised up by the אבנט, and the אבנט cuts them short, then 'raised up' is still difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל's problem was solved by רמי בר חמא. Now the גמרא turns to רב, who says both kinds are פסול, and shows that the ברייתא, which says both are כשר, still contradicts him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One could save the word מרושלין for רב by saying it means long garments pulled up by the אבנט, since the belt counts as cutting off the extra. But the word מסולקין (garments of the right length that were pulled up) is still called כשר in the ברייתא, while רב calls מסולקין פסול. So the contradiction is not fully solved.

keyTerms.meaning: The belt the כהן wears around his garments
It surely cuts (the belt counts as trimming the extra length)
And if you will say (the גמרא tries out a possible answer)

phrases.english: But for רב it is difficult!
And if you will say: what is meant by 'dragging'?
Garments raised up by means of the belt
And the belt surely cuts them short;
phrases.notes: Literally 'cutting, it cuts.' Pulling the extra up with the belt counts as if the extra were cut off.

phrases.english: But then 'raised up' is difficult!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתא was settled for שמואל, the גמרא now applies the same ברייתא against רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that both מרושלין and מסולקין are פסול
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא calls both כשר. Even if מרושלין is reread to fit רב, the separate word מסולקין still contradicts him.

steps.title: רב read the ברייתא as one single case
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא explains that רב's version of the ברייתא was one combined case: dragging garments that were pulled up with the אבנט are כשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: רב taught it as one case: dragging garments that he raised up by means of the belt are כשר.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers the problem from step 8 by saying רב did not read the ברייתא as two separate cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב's version there is no separate clause saying מסולקין are כשר. The ברייתא only says that garments that were too long and then pulled up to the right length are כשר. Anything that ends up too long or too short stays פסול, so the ברייתא no longer contradicts רב.

keyTerms.meaning: He taught it as one (one combined case, not two)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read מרושלין and מסולקין here as two cases. In רב's version they describe the same garment: too long, then pulled up.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said
Rav taught it as one:
Dragging garments that he raised up
By means of the belt are valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא רַב חֲדָא תָּנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא against רב from step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different version of the ברייתא's wording (one case instead of two)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא lists two separate cases, מרושלין and מסולקין, and calls both כשר
steps.terutzMaskana: For רב, the ברייתא speaks of one case: long garments pulled up by the אבנט to the right length are כשר
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל is defended by רמי בר חמא's reading, and רב is defended by רבי זירא's reading. Each has his own way to fit the ברייתא.

steps.title: Unraised long garments depend on a תנאים dispute
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה מדיפתי says that the case of dragging garments that were never pulled up is a dispute between תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה מדיפתי said: dragging garments that were not raised up are a dispute of תנאים.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement opens here. רבי ירמיה מדיפתי says the case of too-long garments left hanging is already argued about by תנאים, and he is about to show the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion was about garments that were pulled up. Here the focus is garments that stayed too long. רבי ירמיה claims this depends on a deeper argument between תנאים, which the next steps will show.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a dispute between תנאים
That he did not raise up

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti said:
Dragging garments that he did not raise up –
It is a dispute of tanna'im,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from pulled-up garments to garments left too long, and ties them to a תנאים dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether unraised long בגדי כהונה are כשר is a dispute between תנאים.

steps.title: First ברייתא: a five-cornered garment needs ציצית
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the פסוק that a three-cornered garment is exempt from ציצית, but a five-cornered garment is obligated, because five corners include four.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'On the four corners of your garment' means four and not three. Maybe it means four and not five? Since it says 'with which you cover yourself,' a five-cornered garment is included. So 'four' means four and not three. Why include five and exclude three? Five includes four, but three does not include four.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the first of two sources רבי ירמיה brings to show the תנאים dispute. This תנא says a five-cornered garment does need ציצית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'four' could exclude both three and five. But the extra words 'with which you cover yourself' widen the law, so the ברייתא includes five and excludes only three. The reason: a five-cornered garment still has four corners inside it, while a three-cornered garment does not.

phrases.english: As it was taught: 'On the four corners of your garment' –
Four and not three.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא אַרְבַּע וְלֹא חָמֵשׁ?
phrases.english: Or perhaps it is only four and not five?
When it says 'with which you cover yourself' –
phrases.notes: Same פסוק, דברים 22:12. Any garment you cover yourself with is included, even one with five corners.

phrases.english: A five-cornered garment is mentioned;
So how do I fulfill the word 'four'?
Four and not three.
And what did you see to include a five-cornered garment
And to exclude a three-cornered garment?
I include a five-cornered garment –
Since four is included within five,
And I exclude a three-cornered garment –
Since four is not included within three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the first source for רבי ירמיה's claim that there is a תנאים dispute.
steps.raayaObject: That תנאים argue about something with extra beyond the required amount
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא ruling that a five-cornered garment needs ציצית

steps.title: Second ברייתא: only exactly four corners
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא learns from the same פסוק that only a garment with exactly four corners needs ציצית: not three and not five.
steps.simpleTranslation: And another ברייתא taught: 'On the four corners of your garment' means four and not three, four and not five.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second source. This תנא disagrees with the first one and exempts a five-cornered garment from ציצית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now we have two ברייתות on the same פסוק with opposite results for five corners. This sets up רבי ירמיה's next move: explaining what the two תנאים are really arguing about.

phrases.english: And another baraita taught:
'On the four corners of your garment' –
Four and not three,
Four and not five.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the opposite ברייתא, completing the two sides of the dispute.
steps.raayaObject: That there is a real dispute about a five-cornered garment
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא exempting a five-cornered garment from ציצית

steps.title: The dispute: does something extra count as being there?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה suggests the two ברייתות argue whether an extra part is treated as if it is there or as if it is not there. That same question decides whether long, unraised בגדי כהונה are כשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it that they argue about this: one master holds that something extra is considered as if it is there, and the other master holds it is considered as if it is not there?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה finishes his proposed proof by suggesting the idea behind the two ברייתות, which would link them to the long garments of the כהן. The next step rejects this suggestion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא who exempts five corners holds the extra corner counts, so the garment is not a 'four-cornered' garment. The תנא who obligates holds the extra is ignored, so it is just four corners. The same goes for a כהן's garment that is too long: if the extra counts, it is פסול; if the extra is ignored, it is כשר.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not that...? (the גמרא suggests an explanation)
Something extra, beyond what is needed
It is considered as if it is there
It is considered as if it is not there

steps.whatToRemember: רבי ירמיה's suggestion: the ציצית dispute is about יתר (does something extra count or get ignored?), and the same question would decide long בגדי כהונה. Step 14 rejects this suggestion.
steps.whyThisMatters: If this suggestion held, the question of long, unraised בגדי כהונה could be traced back to a dispute between תנאים. The next step tests this and rejects it.

phrases.english: What, is it not that they argue about this –

phrases.aramaic: דְּמָר סָבַר: יָתֵר כְּמַאן דְּאִיתֵיהּ דָּמֵי,
phrases.english: That one master holds: something extra is considered as if it is there,
phrases.notes: This is the second ברייתא's view, so the fifth corner counts and the garment is exempt.

phrases.english: And the other master holds: it is considered as if it is not there?
phrases.notes: This is the first ברייתא's view, so the extra corner is ignored and the garment needs ציצית.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the two ברייתות and ties it to רבי ירמיה's claim in step 10.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Proposed (and rejected in step 14): the ציצית dispute is about whether יתר counts as if it is there, which would also decide whether long, unraised בגדי כהונה are כשר.

steps.title: Everyone agrees an extra part counts; the פסוק makes ציצית different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רבי ירמיה's idea. Both ברייתות agree that an extra part counts as if it is there. The view that obligates five corners relies on a special extra word in the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees an extra part is treated as if it is there. But ציצית is different, because the Torah added more with the words "with which you cover yourself."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי ירמיה's suggestion that the two ברייתות argue about whether an extra part counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If an extra part counts, then a five-cornered garment is not a plain four-cornered garment, so on its own it would be exempt. The view that obligates it learns this from the extra words ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״, not from a general rule. So the ציצית argument is not a תנאים dispute about extra parts: both תנאים hold that extra length counts, which would make long, unraised garments פסול.

keyTerms.meaning: It is treated as if it is there
The Torah (literally, the Merciful One) included it

steps.confusionAlert: The word רַבִּי here is not the title "רבי." It is a verb meaning "included" or "added."
steps.whyThisMatters: This removes רבי ירמיה's proof that long, unraised בגדי כהונה are a תנאים dispute. Both ציצית תנאים hold that the extra length counts.

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees
that it is treated as if it is there;
but here it is different,
because the Torah included it:
"with which you cover yourself."

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא כְּמַאן דְּאִיתֵיהּ דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the explanation offered in step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבי ירמיה's claim that the two ברייתות argue about whether an extra part counts.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The view that obligates five corners relies on an extra word in the פסוק, not on a general rule that an extra part does not count.

steps.title: How does the other view use ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the view that exempts five corners learns from the words ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other view: what does he do with "with which you cover yourself"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question. If one view uses these words to include five corners, the other view must use them for something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes no words in the Torah are extra. The view that exempts five corners still has to explain what ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other view)
What does he do with it? (what does he learn from it?)

phrases.english: And the other one,
phrases.notes: This is the view that says a five-cornered garment is exempt.

phrases.english: this "with which you cover yourself",
what does he do with it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, הַאי אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ מַאי עָבֵיד לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on step 14 by asking about the other view's use of the same פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the view that exempts five corners learns from ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״.

steps.title: He uses it to include a blind person's garment
steps.stepSummary: The other view uses ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ to obligate a blind person's garment, as a ברייתא teaches. ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ then excludes only a night garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs it for what a ברייתא teaches. "And you shall see it" leaves out a night garment. Maybe it leaves out a blind person's garment instead? No, because "with which you cover yourself" already includes a blind person's garment. So "and you shall see it" must leave out a night garment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by quoting a ברייתא. It uses ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ to include a blind person's garment in ציצית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ could seem to leave out a blind person, who cannot see. But ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ includes any garment a person covers himself with, even a blind person's. So the seeing-words must leave out something else: a garment worn only at night.

keyTerms.meaning: How do I give meaning to (this פסוק)?

phrases.english: He needs it for what was taught in a ברייתא:
"and you shall see it"
leaves out a night garment.
Or perhaps it only
leaves out a blind person's garment?
When it says, "with which you cover yourself,"
a blind person's garment is already included,
so what do I do with "and you shall see it"?
It leaves out a night garment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He uses ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ to include a blind person's garment in ציצית.

steps.title: Why include the blind person and not the night garment?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks why we include a blind person's garment and leave out a night garment, rather than the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what made you include a blind person's garment and leave out a night garment?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges its own choice. It is setting up the next line, which explains the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both garments seem to lack "seeing": the blind person cannot see, and at night nobody can see. So why should ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ include one and ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ leave out the other?

keyTerms.meaning: What made you decide? (literally, what did you see?)

phrases.english: And what made you decide
to include a blind person's garment
and to leave out a night garment?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא by questioning the choice made in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for including a blind person's garment and leaving out a night garment.

steps.title: Others can see the blind person's ציצית
steps.stepSummary: A blind person's ציצית can still be seen by other people, but a night garment cannot be seen by anyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: I include a blind person's garment because other people can see it. I leave out a night garment because even other people cannot see it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question. "Seeing" can be done by other people, not only by the wearer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ציצית of a blind person are still seen by others, so they still fulfill ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ in some way. At night nobody sees them, so a night garment is the one that is left out.

keyTerms.meaning: Able to be seen by other people

phrases.english: I include a blind person's garment
because other people can see it,
and I leave out a night garment
because even other people cannot see it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A blind person's garment can be seen by others; a night garment cannot be seen by anyone.

steps.title: The first view learns the blind person's garment from ״אֲשֶׁר״
steps.stepSummary: The view that obligates five corners uses ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ for five corners. He learns the blind person's garment from the single word ״אֲשֶׁר״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other view? He learns it from the word "which."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the view that obligates five corners and asks, in very short form, where he learns the blind person's garment. It answers: from the word ״אֲשֶׁר״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This view already used ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ to include a five-cornered garment. So he needs a separate source for the blind person's garment. He finds it in the extra word ״אֲשֶׁר״ on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: "Which", read here as a word that adds something

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: Now it means the view that obligates five corners. The גמרא is asking where he learns the blind person's garment.

phrases.english: He learns it from "which."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns back to the view from step 14 to explain where he learns the law of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The view that obligates five corners learns the blind person's garment from the word ״אֲשֶׁר״.

steps.title: The other view does not learn from ״אֲשֶׁר״
steps.stepSummary: The view that exempts five corners does not learn anything from the word ״אֲשֶׁר״, so he needs the whole phrase for the blind person's garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other view? He does not learn anything from "which."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the topic by explaining why the view that exempts five corners cannot use ״אֲשֶׁר״ the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two views really argue about how to read the פסוק: does the single word ״אֲשֶׁר״ teach something on its own? That is the true reason for their disagreement about five corners. It has nothing to do with whether an extra part counts.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not learn anything from (that word)

steps.whatToRemember: Both ציצית תנאים hold that an extra part counts as if it is there, so רבי ירמיה's תנאים dispute about long, unraised בגדי כהונה falls away. The argument about a five-cornered garment comes from how each view reads ״אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ״ and the word ״אֲשֶׁר״.

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: Back to the view that exempts five corners: why doesn't he use ״אֲשֶׁר״ for the blind person?

phrases.english: He does not learn anything from "which."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the matching question about the other view and closes the discussion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The views argue about whether the word ״אֲשֶׁר״ teaches something, not about whether an extra part counts. So the ציצית ברייתות do not show a תנאים dispute about long, unraised בגדי כהונה.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists what the word ״בַּד״ teaches about priestly garments
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says the word ״בַּד″ teaches five things: the garments are of fine linen, new, twisted, with six-ply thread, and the כהן may not wear ordinary clothes with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: ״בַּד״ teaches that the garments are made of fine linen. ״בַּד״ teaches that they are new. ״בַּד״ teaches that their threads are twisted. ״בַּד״ teaches that each thread is folded six times. ״בַּד״ teaches that the כהן may not wear ordinary clothes together with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that draws five rules about the כהן's garments from the repeated word ״בַּד״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each rule is attached to the same word, ״בַּד״. At first glance it looks like every rule comes straight from the פסוק, so every rule would seem to be a strict requirement. The next steps question exactly that point.

keyTerms.meaning: Linen; the material of the כהן's garments

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"Linen": that they must be of fine linen;
"Linen": that they must be new;
"Linen": that they must be twisted;
"Linen": that their thread must be folded six times;
"Linen": that he may not wear ordinary clothes with them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: the material and features of the בגדי כהונה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word ״בַּד״ is linked to five features of the כהן's garments.

steps.title: אביי asks how ״new″ can be a requirement
steps.stepSummary: אביי accepts the rule of fine linen. But if ״new″ is required, worn-out garments should be invalid, and a ברייתא says they are valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב יוסף: The rule that they must be fine linen makes sense. It teaches that fine linen is valid and other materials are not. But ״בַּד״ teaching that they must be new would mean new is valid and worn-out is not. Doesn't a ברייתא teach that worn-out garments are valid?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges the ברייתא: one of its rules seems to contradict another ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every rule in the list comes from the פסוק, every rule should be required. ״Fine linen only″ fits that reading. ״New only″ does not, because an earlier ברייתא allows worn-out garments.

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Yosef:
Granted, that they must be of fine linen:
this teaches us
that fine linen, yes; something else, no.
But "linen" teaching that they must be new:
new, yes, but worn-out, no?!
But isn't it taught: worn-out ones are valid!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges one item in the ברייתא's list.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If ״new″ comes from the פסוק, it should be required. Yet worn-out garments are valid.

steps.title: רב יוסף shows the same problem with ״six-ply thread″
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers with a question of his own: ״בַּד״ means ״single,″ so how could it teach a thread folded six times?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said to him: According to your reasoning, how can ״בַּד״ teach that the thread is folded six times? ״בַּד״ means each one on its own!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף does not answer directly yet. He shows that אביי's reading of the ברייתא causes an even bigger problem, which sets up his real answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we read every rule as coming straight from the word ״בַּד,״ the six-fold thread makes no sense, because ״בַּד״ means single. So the ברייתא must not mean that each rule is learned from the word itself.
steps.confusionAlert: רב יוסף is not disagreeing that the thread is six-ply. He is showing that this rule cannot come from the meaning of the word ״בַּד.״

phrases.english: He said to him: And according to your reasoning,
"linen" teaches that their thread must be folded six times?!
"Bad" means each one on its own!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Counters אביי's question by showing that his reading of the ברייתא fails anyway.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's assumption that every rule is learned from the word ״בַּד״
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ״בַּד״ means single, so it cannot be the source for a six-ply thread.

steps.title: The real meaning: some features are ideal, some are required
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is describing ״בַּד״ garments. Some of the features are a מצוה to do from the start, and some are required for the garment to be valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what the ברייתא means: garments that are called ״בַּד״ need to be of fine linen, new, twisted, and with thread folded six times. Some of these are the proper way to do the מצוה, and some are required for the garment to be valid.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives his answer: the ברייתא is a description of the garments, not a list of rules learned one by one from the word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answers אביי. ״New″ is only the ideal way, so worn-out garments are still valid. ״Fine linen″ can still be a required feature, so not every item on the list carries the same weight.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this is what it means
The proper way to do it from the start, but not required
Required; without it the garment is invalid

steps.whatToRemember: Some features of the ״בַּד״ garments are only ideal (like being new). Others are required (like fine linen).

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it is saying:
Garments about which "linen" is said
need to be of fine linen,
new, twisted,
and their thread folded six times;

phrases.aramaic: יֵשׁ מֵהֶן לְמִצְוָה, יֵשׁ מֵהֶן לְעַכֵּב.
phrases.english: some of them are the proper way, and some of them are required.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the real answer to אביי's question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the ברייתא as a description, with features of different strength
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each rule comes from the word ״בַּד״ and is required.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא describes ״בַּד״ garments; some features are ideal and some are required, so worn-out garments are valid.

steps.title: How do we know ״בַּד״ is flax?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that the material called ״בַּד״ is flax.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know that this ״בַּד״ is flax?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a basic question about what material the word ״בַּד״ refers to. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now everyone assumed ״בַּד״ means linen. The גמרא now wants a reason from the word itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Flax, the plant linen is made from

phrases.english: From where do we know that this "bad" is flax?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the features of the garments to what ״בַּד״ itself means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that ״בַּד״ refers to flax.

steps.title: Flax grows one stalk at a time
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסף בר רבי חנינא explains that ״בַּד״ refers to a plant that grows from the ground one stalk on its own, and flax fits this.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסף בר רבי חנינא said: It is something that grows from the ground with each stalk on its own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ״בַּד״ (single) describes a plant whose stalks grow separately, one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This uses the same meaning of ״בַּד״ that רב יוסף used earlier: single, alone. Flax grows as separate single stalks that do not split, so it matches the word.

keyTerms.meaning: Each one on its own, one by one

steps.whatToRemember: ״בַּד״ means single. That is why it refers to flax, a plant whose stalks grow one by one.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosef, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:

phrases.aramaic: דָּבָר הָעוֹלֶה מִן הַקַּרְקַע בַּד בְּבַד.
phrases.english: An item that grows from the ground each one on its own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of how we know ״בַּד״ is flax.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״בַּד״ refers to a plant that grows single stalk by single stalk, which is flax.

steps.title: Why not say the material is wool?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof from 'one stalk on its own' by suggesting that wool might fit that description too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say it is wool!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוסף בר רבי חנינא's proof. Maybe wool also counts as something that comes 'one by one,' so ״בַּד״ could mean wool.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 26 said ״בַּד״ is something that grows one stalk on its own. The גמרא asks why that must mean flax. Each strand of wool also grows separately, so wool might fit the definition just as well.

phrases.english: Say it is wool!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof that 'one stalk on its own' points only to flax.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 26 that ״בַּד״ must be flax
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Wool may also match the 'single, on its own' description, so the proof does not single out flax.

steps.title: Wool splits, so it is not 'single'
steps.stepSummary: Wool cannot be ״בַּד״ because its fibers split.
steps.simpleTranslation: Wool splits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that wool does not fit, because its strands split into smaller strands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״בַּד״ means something single and unbranched. A wool fiber divides into smaller fibers, so it is not truly 'one on its own.' That rules wool out.

phrases.english: Wool splits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wool challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes wool from flax by a physical feature
steps.terutzMaskana: Wool splits, so it is not 'single' and cannot be ״בַּד״.

steps.title: But flax splits too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that flax also splits, so the same reason should rule out flax.
steps.simpleTranslation: Flax also splits!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: if splitting disqualifies wool, it should disqualify flax as well, since flax also splits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 28 used splitting to tell wool and flax apart. But flax fibers also come apart into thinner strands. So that difference seems to fall away.

phrases.english: Flax also splits!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the difference given in step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that splitting is what separates wool from flax
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Flax also splits, so splitting cannot be the difference between them.

steps.title: Flax splits only when it is beaten
steps.stepSummary: Flax splits only through beating, while wool splits on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: It splits only by being struck.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that flax splits only when someone beats it. In its natural state it stays single.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference is natural splitting versus splitting caused by processing. Wool splits by itself, so it is not 'single.' Flax is naturally single and comes apart only when it is struck, so it still fits ״בַּד״.
steps.whatToRemember: ״בַּד״ is flax because flax grows as a single stalk and splits only when beaten. Wool splits on its own.

phrases.english: It splits only by being struck.
phrases.notes: Flax is beaten during processing to separate its fibers. Left alone, it stays as one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge that flax also splits.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Refines the distinction: natural splitting versus splitting caused by processing
steps.terutzMaskana: Flax splits only when beaten, so in its natural state it is single and fits ״בַּד״.

steps.title: רבינא's proof from יחזקאל
steps.stepSummary: רבינא brings a different source: יחזקאל calls the כהנים' clothes ״פִשְׁתִּים״, which means flax.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא says it comes from here: 'They shall have linen crowns on their heads, and linen pants on their waists; they shall not gird themselves with ״יזע״.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers another way to prove that the כהנים' clothes are flax. He quotes a פסוק in יחזקאל that says it openly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of explaining the word ״בַּד״, רבינא points to a פסוק that uses the clear word ״פִשְׁתִּים״, flax. This gives a direct source with no need to analyze how flax grows.

phrases.english: Ravina says: from here:
"They shall have linen crowns upon their heads,
and shall have linen breeches upon their loins;
they shall not gird themselves with yaza."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the question in step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק in יחזקאל openly says the כהנים' clothes are made of flax.

steps.title: What was the source before יחזקאל?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks how people knew the clothes were flax before יחזקאל lived.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to רבינא: But before יחזקאל came, from where did we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי challenges רבינא. יחזקאל lived long after משה, so how did כהנים know to use flax before his time?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נביא cannot create a new Torah law. Earlier generations of כהנים needed to know the law already. So יחזקאל's פסוק cannot be the real origin of the rule.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to Ravina:
But until Ezekiel came, from where did we derive it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's source.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's use of a פסוק in יחזקאל as the source
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The law applied before יחזקאל, so his words cannot be its original source.

steps.title: A tradition that יחזקאל attached to a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבינא replies that the same question applies to רב חסדא's rule. The answer for both is that the law was a tradition, and יחזקאל only gave it a פסוק for support.
steps.simpleTranslation: And by your reasoning, what about רב חסדא's statement: 'We did not learn this from the Torah of משה רבינו; we learned it from the words of יחזקאל בן בוזי: No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart or uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter My מקדש to serve Me.' Before יחזקאל came, from where did we know that? Rather, it was learned as a tradition, and יחזקאל came and leaned it on a פסוק. Here too, it was learned as a tradition, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers by pointing to רב חסדא, who also said a law comes from יחזקאל. In both cases the law was really a tradition, and יחזקאל only supported it with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא shows that רב אשי's question would also hit רב חסדא's well-known statement. The answer that works for רב חסדא works here too: the law was an oral tradition from earlier times. יחזקאל did not invent it; he only connected it to a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: It was learned as a tradition
He leaned it on a פסוק (gave it support from a verse)

steps.whatToRemember: Some laws first written in the נביאים were really older traditions. The נביא only attached them to a פסוק.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think יחזקאל created a new law. The law already existed as a tradition; he gave it a פסוק to lean on.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains how laws that appear in the נביאים can still be binding from earlier times: they were oral traditions given written support.

phrases.english: And according to your reasoning, that which Rav Ḥisda said:

phrases.aramaic: דָּבָר זֶה – מִתּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ לֹא לָמַדְנוּ,
phrases.english: This matter we did not learn from the Torah of Moses, our teacher;
we learned it from the words of Ezekiel, son of Buzi:

phrases.aramaic: ״כׇּל בֶּן נֵכָר עֶרֶל לֵב וְעֶרֶל בָּשָׂר
phrases.english: "No stranger, uncircumcised in heart or uncircumcised in flesh,
shall enter into My Sanctuary to serve Me";
until Ezekiel came, from where did we derive it?
Rather, it was learned as a tradition,
and Ezekiel came and supported it with a verse;

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי גְּמָרָא גְּמִירִי לַהּ כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: here too, it was learned as a tradition, etc.
phrases.notes: "Etc." stands for the rest: and יחזקאל came and supported it with a פסוק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Comparison to an accepted case (רב חסדא) plus redefining the role of the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יחזקאל's פסוק is the original source, so the law could not have been known before him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The law was a tradition from earlier times; יחזקאל only gave it support from a פסוק.

steps.title: What does ״לֹא יַחְגְּרוּ בַּיָּזַע״ mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the meaning of the unclear phrase ״לֹא יַחְגְּרוּ בַּיָּזַע״.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of ״לֹא יַחְגְּרוּ בַּיָּזַע״ (they shall not gird themselves with ״יָזַע״)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the last phrase of רבינא's פסוק and asks what it means. This sets up אביי's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ״יָּזַע״ is rare and unclear. The גמרא wants to know what it tells the כהן to avoid when he ties his belt.

phrases.english: What is the meaning of "they shall not gird themselves with yaza"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up an unclear phrase from the פסוק quoted in step 31.

steps.title: אביי: not where people sweat
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the כהנים must not tie the belt at a place on the body where people sweat.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: They shall not tie the belt at a place where people sweat.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers that ״יָּזַע״ means sweat. The כהן should not tie his belt at a sweaty spot on the body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי reads ״יָּזַע״ as connected to ״מְזִיעִין״, sweating. The rule is about where the belt sits on the body, not what it is made of.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
They shall not gird themselves in a place where people sweat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי לָא יַחְגְּרוּ בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁמְּזִיעִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 34.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״יָּזַע״ means sweat: the belt may not be tied at a sweaty place on the body.

steps.title: A ברייתא about where the belt is tied
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports אביי: the belt may not be tied below the waist or above the elbows, but rather... (the sentence continues on the next amud).
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: When they tie the belt, they may not tie it below their waists, nor above their elbows, but rather...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up אביי's explanation. The quote stops at 'but rather' and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists places where the belt may not go: too low (below the waist) and too high (above the elbows). These are sweaty spots, which fits אביי's reading. The allowed place comes next in the text.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As it is taught in a baraita:
When they gird themselves,
they may not gird themselves below their loins,
nor above their elbows, but rather

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports אביי's explanation in step 35.
steps.raayaObject: אביי's reading that ״יָּזַע״ means a place where people sweat
